paragraphs: Before reciting the blessing of Hagomel, one should say the verse (Psalms 111:1), "I will thank the Lord with all my heart, in the council of the upright and the assembly." Afterward he recites the blessing, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who bestows good things on the guilty, who has bestowed on me all good." Those who hear it say, "May He who bestowed on you all good bestow on you all good forever." And he answers after them, "Amen, so may it be His will."

clarification.explanation: Before the blessing of Hagomel one recites the verse "I will thank the Lord with all my heart, in the council of the upright and the assembly." Afterward one recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who bestows good things on the guilty, who has bestowed on me all good." Those who hear it respond, "May He who bestowed on you all good bestow on you all good forever," and the one reciting the blessing answers after them, "Amen, so may it be His will."
takeaways: The verse "I will thank the Lord with all my heart" is said before the blessing.
Those who hear it respond, "May He who bestowed on you... bestow on you all good forever," and the one blessing answers Amen.

paragraphs: One must recite the blessing in the presence of ten, two of whom have studied halachah [are Torah scholars]. It is good to be careful that there be twelve together with the one reciting the blessing, including the two scholars mentioned. And if two who have studied halachah are not available, he should nevertheless recite the blessing, and the blessing should not be omitted on this account. The custom is to recite it after the public Torah reading, since two who have studied halachah are usually present there. If he recited it in the presence of fewer than ten, some say he has not fulfilled his obligation and some say he has; it is good to go back and recite it in the presence of ten without [God's] name and sovereignty, but rather think the name and sovereignty in his heart. And one who recites the blessing in a whisper is considered as though he recited it not in the presence of ten, and in this case too he must repeat it aloud in the presence of ten without name and sovereignty, only thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One recites the blessing of Hagomel in the presence of ten, two of whom should be Torah scholars; and it is good to be careful that there be twelve together with the one reciting the blessing and the two scholars. If there are no two Torah scholars present, he should nevertheless recite the blessing, and the blessing should not be omitted on this account. The custom is to recite it after the public Torah reading, since Torah scholars are usually present then. If he recited it in the presence of fewer than ten, some say he has not fulfilled his obligation, so it is good to go back and recite it in the presence of ten without [God's] name and sovereignty (thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart). One who recites it in a whisper is also considered as though he recited it not in the presence of ten, and must repeat it aloud in the presence of ten without name and sovereignty.
takeaways: One blesses in the presence of ten, preferably with two Torah scholars among them; the custom is to do so after the Torah reading.

If he blessed in the presence of fewer than ten, or in a whisper, he repeats the blessing aloud in the presence of ten without [God's] name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.

paragraphs: The ten sit, as it is written, "and in the assembly of elders they shall praise Him," while the one reciting the blessing stands, because this blessing takes the place of the thanksgiving offering, and the one who offers it stands and offers it. Therefore the blessing of Hagomel is not recited at night, only during the day; but after the fact, if he recited it at night, he has fulfilled his obligation — see the Chatam Sofer, Orach Chaim, siman 51.

clarification.explanation: The ten sit (as it is said, "and in the assembly of elders they shall praise Him"), while the one reciting the blessing stands — because this blessing takes the place of the thanksgiving offering, and the one who offers a sacrifice stands while offering it. For this reason the blessing of Hagomel is not recited at night, only during the day; but after the fact, if one recited it at night, he has fulfilled his obligation.
takeaways: The one reciting the blessing stands while those listening sit (the blessing takes the place of the thanksgiving offering).
The blessing is recited during the day, not at night; if recited at night, one has fulfilled the obligation after the fact.

paragraphs: A minor under thirteen years of age, once he has reached the age of [religious] training, must recite the blessing. And although there are those who disagree, nevertheless, in a place where there is a custom to recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty, he should recite it with name and sovereignty; and in a place where there is no known custom, he should recite it without name and sovereignty, out of deference to the view of those who disagree.

clarification.explanation: A minor under the age of thirteen who has reached the age of [religious] training must recite the blessing of Hagomel. Although there are those who disagree, in a place where there is a custom to recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty, he should recite it with name and sovereignty; and in a place where there is no clear custom, he should recite it without name and sovereignty, out of deference to the view of those who disagree.
takeaways: A minor who has reached the age of [religious] training recites Hagomel.
With [God's] name and sovereignty where that is the custom; without name and sovereignty where there is no clear custom.

paragraphs: Women are obligated in the blessing of Hagomel, and should recite it in the presence of ten so as to recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty. And if it is difficult for her to recite it in the presence of ten because of embarrassment, she should recite it without name and sovereignty. And if she does not know it, her husband or someone else should teach her, for it is a short blessing.

clarification.explanation: Women are obligated in the blessing of Hagomel, and should recite it in the presence of ten so as to recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty. If it is difficult for a woman to recite it in the presence of ten because of embarrassment, she should recite it without name and sovereignty. And if she does not know [the text of] the blessing, her husband or someone else should teach it to her, since it is a short blessing.
takeaways: Women are obligated in the blessing of Hagomel, and recite it in the presence of ten with [God's] name and sovereignty.
Because of embarrassment — without name and sovereignty; and one who does not know it is taught it.

paragraphs: One who was ill in his eyes and was healed should, according to the law, recite the blessing, but the custom has not been to do so. In any case, he should recite it in the presence of ten without [God's] name and sovereignty, but think the name and sovereignty in his heart — see Ikarei HaDat, letter 24, and other later authorities. It is good that before the blessing he say these three verses, "And David blessed the Lord in the sight of all the assembly...," "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness, etc.," "and the riches and the honor, etc." — and afterward recite the blessing of Hagomel without name and sovereignty. See Pitchei Teshuvah, Yoreh De'ah, siman 328, small section 1, what he wrote in the name of Rabbi Peri Tevuah, what he received from his teachers — look there.

clarification.explanation: One who was ill in his eyes and was healed should, according to the strict law, recite the blessing of Hagomel, but the custom has not been to do so. In any case he should recite it in the presence of ten without [God's] name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart. And it is good that he say beforehand three verses ("And David blessed the Lord in the sight of all the assembly," "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness," "and the riches and the honor"), and afterward recite the blessing without name and sovereignty.
takeaways: One who recovered from an eye ailment recites the blessing in the presence of ten, without [God's] name and sovereignty (thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart).
It is good to precede it with the three verses, "And David blessed..."

paragraphs: For minor ailments, such as a headache and the like, which are not an illness affecting the whole body, one does not recite the blessing. One is not called "ill" for the purpose of reciting the blessing unless he has been confined to bed for three days, and these need not be three full days from time to time [a full 72-hour period].

clarification.explanation: For minor ailments — such as a headache and the like — which are not an illness affecting the entire body, one does not recite the blessing of Hagomel. A person is not considered "ill" for purposes of the blessing unless he has been confined to bed for three days; and these need not be three full days measured from hour to hour.
takeaways: Minor ailments do not obligate the blessing of Hagomel.
One is considered ill only if confined to bed for about three days (not necessarily a full 72-hour period).

paragraphs: One who has a fever that comes at set times, and he sweats and afterward stands on his feet as healthy, and it recurs again, heaven forbid — such a person should not recite the blessing during the sweat that occurs between one bout of fever and the next, but should wait until he is completely saved, so that that heat will not return, drive it away, and go. And he must wait until three periods [onot] have passed, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim and the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: One who has a fever that recurs at set times, and sweats, and after the sweating stands on his feet as though healthy, and the fever then returns, heaven forbid — such a person should not recite [the blessing of Hagomel for his rescue] during the sweat that occurs between one bout of fever and the next, but should wait until he is completely cured, so that the heat will not return again; and he must wait until three periods [onot] have passed (as brought in Chesed LeAlafim and the later authorities).
takeaways: One suffering from recurrent fever does not recite Hagomel during the remission between one attack and the next.
He waits until he is completely cured — after three periods [onot] have passed.

paragraphs: Every prisoner is obligated to recite the blessing upon his release, whether he was imprisoned over a capital matter or over a monetary matter, and even if he was imprisoned over payment of a tax; and likewise even if he was imprisoned over a debt which he had the means to pay but rebelled with force, or thought that because of his imprisonment they would come to a settlement with him — all these are included in the category of "prisoner," and the Sages did not distinguish between them. See Berchei Yosef in the name of our teacher Maharai Migash, who concluded that the custom is that every kind of prisoner blesses upon his release.

clarification.explanation: Every prisoner is obligated to recite Hagomel upon his release from prison — whether he was imprisoned over a capital matter or a monetary matter, and even if imprisoned over payment of a tax, and even if he could have paid but refused, or hoped that because of the imprisonment they would settle with him — all of these are included in the category of "prisoner," and the Sages did not distinguish between them.
takeaways: Anyone released from imprisonment recites Hagomel, regardless of the reason for the imprisonment.

paragraphs: It is specifically for these four — the sick, the imprisoned, [those who cross] the sea, and [those who cross] the desert — that the Sages instituted the recitation of the blessing of Hagomel with [God's] name and sovereignty. But if a wall fell on him, or he fell from a ladder, or the like, among other dangers, and he was saved, he should recite the blessing of Hagomel without name and sovereignty — but he should recite it in the presence of ten. And it is good that in this case too he do as I wrote above in letter 6 [vav], that he say before the blessing the three verses, "And David blessed, etc.," "Yours, O Lord, etc.," "and the riches and the honor, etc."

clarification.explanation: Only for these four — the sick, the imprisoned, those who go down to the sea, and those who travel in the desert — did the Sages institute reciting Hagomel with [God's] name and sovereignty. But one who was saved from some other danger (a wall fell on him, he fell from a ladder, and the like) recites Hagomel without name and sovereignty, though still in the presence of ten. And it is good that here too he precede it with the three verses, "And David blessed..."
takeaways: [God's] name and sovereignty apply only to these four: the sick, the imprisoned, the sea, the desert.
One saved from another kind of danger recites the blessing in the presence of ten, without name and sovereignty.

paragraphs: One for whom a miracle occurred in some place — something that goes beyond the ordinary course of nature — such as a wall or ceiling or large stone falling on him and the like, which in the ordinary course of nature should have caused his death, and he was saved from death — such a person recites, every time he arrives at that place, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who performed a miracle for me in this place." And all his descendants likewise recite the blessing with [God's] name and sovereignty, "who performed a miracle for our father in this place." This applies when there are thirty days between one seeing [of the place] and the next, excluding the day he [first] saw it and excluding the day he currently stands in it; but if he saw it within thirty days, he does not recite the blessing. And if several miracles occurred to him, then upon arriving at one of the places where a miracle occurred to him, he must mention all the miracles of the other places as well, and include everything in one blessing — and this obligation applies specifically to him, but his descendants need not mention the other places.

clarification.explanation: One for whom a supernatural miracle occurred — such as a wall, ceiling, or large stone falling on him, which by the natural order should have caused his death, and he was saved — recites, each time he arrives at that place, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who performed a miracle for me in this place," and his descendants recite "who performed a miracle for our father in this place" (with [God's] name and sovereignty). This is on condition that thirty days have passed between one viewing and the next; within thirty days he does not recite the blessing. And if several miracles occurred to him, then upon reaching one of the places, he mentions all the miracles and includes everything in a single blessing (and this applies specifically to him — his descendants need not mention the other places).
takeaways: A miracle beyond nature — one recites "who performed a miracle for me in this place" (and descendants, "for our father") with [God's] name and sovereignty, at intervals of thirty days.
Multiple miracles are included together in a single blessing.

paragraphs: If thieves came upon him and he was saved, or a stone or piece of iron fell near him — even though he would have been in mortal danger had it fallen on him — he does not recite "who performed a miracle for me," because this does not go beyond the ordinary course of nature. However, if a bullet from a rifle barrel struck him but did not enter his abdomen or the other vital organs, but rather struck his leg or hand; and likewise if someone stabbed him with a knife and the knife did not enter a vital organ but only his flesh — since the object did reach his body, it is in doubt whether he should recite the blessing with [God's] name and sovereignty. Therefore it is good that here too he do as written in letter 6 [vav]: first recite the aforementioned verses three times, and afterward recite the blessing without name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.

clarification.explanation: If thieves came upon him and he was saved, or a stone or piece of iron fell near him (even though he would have been in mortal danger had it fallen on him) — he does not recite "who performed a miracle for me," because this does not go beyond the natural order. But if a bullet struck him in a non-vital spot (his leg or hand), or someone stabbed him with a knife that did not enter a vital organ but only the flesh — since the object did reach his body, there is doubt whether he should recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty; therefore it is good to precede it with the three verses and then recite the blessing without name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.
takeaways: Being saved from a danger within the natural order (thieves, a stone falling nearby) — no blessing for a miracle.
Being struck in a non-vital spot — in doubt, and therefore without [God's] name and sovereignty.

paragraphs: One who sees the sages of Israel recites "Blessed... who has given of His wisdom to those who fear Him," without [God's] name and sovereignty. Likewise, if he sees his friend after twelve months, he recites "who revives the dead," without name and sovereignty. However, we have neither seen nor heard of reciting this blessing over one's friend, even without name and sovereignty, and it is possible this is because people feel uncomfortable being blessed over in this way. Therefore he should think this entire blessing in his heart, in order to fulfill the words of the Sages.

clarification.explanation: One who sees the sages of Israel recites "Blessed... who has given of His wisdom to those who fear Him," without [God's] name and sovereignty. Likewise, one who sees his friend after twelve months recites "who revives the dead," without name and sovereignty. However, in practice the custom has not been to recite this blessing over a friend even without name and sovereignty (perhaps because people feel uncomfortable being blessed over in this way), and therefore he should think the entire blessing in his heart, in order to fulfill the words of the Sages.
takeaways: Seeing the sages of Israel — "who has given of His wisdom to those who fear Him," without [God's] name and sovereignty.
Seeing a friend after twelve months — "who revives the dead"; in practice, one thinks it in his heart.

paragraphs: One who sees his friend, whom he already knows, and thirty days have passed during which he did not see him, and now he is glad to see him, recites "Shehecheyanu." But if he does not know him from before by sight, even though he knows him through letters, he does not recite the blessing. And although according to the strict law he should recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty, since the world has not been accustomed to do so, and there is also some basis for the custom, therefore he should recite it without name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.

clarification.explanation: One who sees his friend whom he already knows, and has not seen him for thirty days, and is now glad to see him, recites "Shehecheyanu." But if he does not know his face (only through letters, for instance), he does not recite the blessing. And although by strict law one should recite it with [God's] name and sovereignty, since the custom has not been so, and there is some basis for the custom, one should recite it without name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart.
takeaways: A joyful meeting with a familiar friend after thirty days — Shehecheyanu (by custom: without [God's] name and sovereignty, thought in the heart).
One does not recite the blessing over someone known only through correspondence.

paragraphs: One who sees graves of Israel recites, with [God's] name and sovereignty, the blessing written in the machzor. But here in our city Baghdad, may it be protected, the custom has not been to recite it even without name and sovereignty, because on the eve of Rosh Hashanah the entire community goes to the cemetery and no blessing is recited at all. Only at a new death, God forbid, does one person recite that blessing with name and sovereignty, aloud, and the assembled mourners who accompany the deceased answer Amen; and they must be informed to intend, both the one who hears and the one who is heard, so as to fulfill their obligation. Also, when people go out on the eve of Rosh Hashanah and at other times, they should be careful to recite it at least without name and sovereignty; and the fact that previously they were not accustomed to recite it even without name and sovereignty is not proof of a valid custom, for one might say that since it was not fluent in their mouths, therefore they did not recite it. And some years ago I printed here in our city a well-corrected cemetery prayer book, and in it I printed this blessing without name and sovereignty, so that it be recited.

clarification.explanation: One who sees graves of Israel recites, with [God's] name and sovereignty, the blessing written in the machzor. But in Baghdad the custom has not been to recite it even without name and sovereignty — on the eve of Rosh Hashanah the whole community goes to the cemetery and no blessing is recited at all. Only at a new burial does one person recite that blessing with name and sovereignty aloud, and those accompanying the deceased answer Amen (and they must intend, both hearer and speaker, so as to fulfill the obligation). It is fitting that one recite it at least without name and sovereignty also on the eve of Rosh Hashanah and at other times. [Rabbi Yosef Chaim] notes that some years earlier he printed here a well-corrected cemetery prayer book, in which he printed this blessing without name and sovereignty, so that it would be recited.
takeaways: One who sees graves of Israel — the blessing with [God's] name and sovereignty, per the machzor.
The custom in Baghdad had been not to recite it; it is fitting to recite it at least without name and sovereignty, and at a new burial one person recites it aloud while the others answer Amen.

paragraphs: For lightning one recites "Blessed... who performs the work of creation," and for thunder one recites "Blessed... whose strength and might fill the world." By strict law one should recite these with [God's] name and sovereignty, but here in our city the custom has been to recite both these blessings without name and sovereignty. And our friend, the great Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may he be blessed, wrote to me that also in the holy cities, may they be rebuilt speedily, the custom is to recite them without name and sovereignty, and he wrote that Rabbi Petach HaDevir, part 2, siman 227, addressed this custom — but that book is not available to us.

clarification.explanation: For lightning one recites "Blessed... who performs the work of creation," and for thunder, "Blessed... whose strength and might fill the world." By strict law these should be recited with [God's] name and sovereignty, but in Baghdad the custom has been to recite both blessings without name and sovereignty, and Rabbi Eliyahu Mani likewise attested that this is also the custom in the holy cities.
takeaways: Lightning — "who performs the work of creation"; thunder — "whose strength and might fill the world."
The custom in Baghdad and in the holy cities is to recite them without [God's] name and sovereignty.

paragraphs: One who sees a rainbow says, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who remembers the covenant, and is faithful to His covenant and true to His word." And it is forbidden to gaze at it. According to the view of the Gaon Maharai, of blessed memory, in Yoreh De'ah, that there are two kinds of rainbows, one would therefore need to recite the blessing without [God's] name and sovereignty, since we cannot know [which kind it is]. However, his remarks, which were stated homiletically, are not sufficient to uproot the custom of Israel to recite it with name and sovereignty, especially since all the great decisors have remained silent on this matter. Nevertheless, one who wishes to be pious and recite it without name and sovereignty, thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart, is not stopped from doing so.

clarification.explanation: One who sees a rainbow says, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who remembers the covenant, and is faithful to His covenant and true to His word," and it is forbidden to gaze at the rainbow. There is a view (stated homiletically) that there are two kinds of rainbows, and that therefore one should recite the blessing without [God's] name and sovereignty; but this is not sufficient to uproot the custom of Israel to recite it with name and sovereignty, following the view of all the great decisors. One who wishes to be stringent and recite it without name and sovereignty (thinking the name and sovereignty in his heart) is not prevented from doing so.
takeaways: One who sees a rainbow recites "who remembers the covenant..." with [God's] name and sovereignty (following the custom), and it is forbidden to gaze at it.

paragraphs: A person should be careful [to recite] the Traveler's Prayer [Tefillat HaDerech], and it is fitting to attach it to some [other] blessing — for example, if he eats or drinks and recites the concluding blessing, he should attach the Traveler's Prayer to it; or he may attach it to the blessing of "Asher Yatzar," if the opportunity arises. And if it is possible to recite it while standing, how good that is; and if not possible, he should recite it while walking. And one recites it only if he is to travel at least a parasah. And if he traveled several parasahs and forgot to recite it, if a parasah's distance remains for him to travel, he should recite it; and one recites it only once a day. And every person setting out on a journey from a city should be careful to make the "accompaniment" [levayah] arrangement, as written in the siddur, gathering with friends, and when he parts from them he should say, "This is the halachah: an individual and the many — the halachah follows the many," and he should intend the initial letters of the holy name Yod-Vav-Heh-Kaf, which is efficacious for protection on the road, as this is alluded to in the final letters of [the verse] "For He will charge His angels concerning you" (Psalms 91:11). And know that I found in [the work] Keter Malchut a written petition and praise to God, founded upon that holy name, that the traveler should say at the time of his travel: "Blessed and praised is He who grants existence to all, glorified and exalted is the Creator of all, uplifted and honored is the Fashioner of all, elevated and praised is He who makes each one unique — You have shown us Your glory, Fashioner and Creator who established Your throne, founded and built the Temple of Your glory, unique and singular, whose glory is praised, Fashioner and Creator whose throne is exalted — may He increase and multiply the strengthening of our power, may He give us strength and may all enemies perish; may He help us and may all foes be cut off; may He guard us and may all accusers be nullified; may He strengthen us and may all prosecutors be nullified. May God make our intention firm and strong; may God make our intention exalted and steadfast; may God bless and better our intention; may God adorn and prosper our intention; may He illuminate and prosper the entire journey; may the journey be made firm and straight according to our will, for good and for blessing, for a good life and for peace. Amen, so may it be His will."

clarification.explanation: A person should be careful [to recite] the Traveler's Prayer. It is fitting to attach it to some [other] blessing — for example, if he eats or drinks and recites the concluding blessing, he should attach the Traveler's Prayer to it, or attach it to the blessing of "Asher Yatzar" if that opportunity arises. If it is possible to recite it standing — how good; if not, he recites it while walking. One recites it only if he is to travel at least a parasah; and if he traveled several parasahs and forgot, and a parasah's distance remains, he should recite it; and it is recited only once a day. Likewise, anyone setting out on a journey from a city should be careful to arrange an "accompaniment" [levayah], as brought in the siddur, gathering with friends, and when parting from them should say, "The halachah is: an individual and the many — the halachah follows the many," and intend the initial letters of the holy name that is efficacious for protection on the road (alluded to in the final letters of "For He will charge His angels concerning you"). The Ben Ish Chai further brings that he found in "Keter Malchut" a petition and praise to God founded on that same holy name, for the traveler to say at the time of his journey ("Blessed and praised is He who grants existence to all... may He illuminate and prosper the entire journey... for a good life and for peace, Amen").
takeaways: The Traveler's Prayer — attach it to another blessing, [recite it] for a distance of a parasah or more, once a day; standing, if possible.

When parting from those accompanying him, he says "an individual and the many — the halachah follows the many" and intends the name Yod-Vav-Heh-Kaf for protection on the road; and there is a petition from "Keter Malchut" to be said while traveling.

paragraphs: One who sees the sun at its [cyclical] turning point [tekufah] — which occurs once every twenty-eight years, the tekufah falling at the start of the night of Wednesday — when he sees it in the morning recites, "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who performs the work of creation," because at that time the sun stands at the point where it stood at the start of its being suspended in the firmament during the work of creation. The time for reciting the blessing with [God's] name and sovereignty is until three seasonal hours [into the day]; and if three seasonal hours have passed, he recites it without name and sovereignty until midday, as the Gaon Chatam Sofer wrote in Orach Chaim, siman 56. And although there are those who hold that one should recite it with name and sovereignty until midday, we follow the rule that in a case of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. And one should be careful to recite the blessing in a place where he can see the disk of the sun itself, and it does not suffice merely to see the light of its rising, as the Machazik Berachah wrote, siman 229, small section 4.

It is a mitzvah to recite this blessing in a gathering of people, because of "In the multitude of people is the King's glory" (Proverbs 14:28), as the later authorities have written. And if there was a cloud, he should not recite the blessing until the cloud passes; and if the cloud does not pass from over it, he recites the blessing without [God's] name and sovereignty — even though there are many who hold that he should recite it with name and sovereignty — since in a case of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient; see the Chatam Sofer there, and his son, the Gaon Ketav Sofer, in Orach Chaim, siman 34. As for women, the Gaon Chatam Sofer raised the question whether they should recite the blessing or not; see his son, the Gaon [author of] Ketav Sofer, there. Therefore the women should come and stand near the men, and when the cantor recites the blessing alone in a loud voice, he should intend to discharge their obligation, and the women should also intend to fulfill their obligation by hearing the blessing. Likewise the cantor should intend [to discharge the obligation of] the blind, and they too should intend to fulfill their obligation. As for the fact that Shehecheyanu is not recited over this mitzvah, the Gaon Ketav Sofer gave a reason for this.

Before the blessing, the congregation and the cantor should stand together in one place on the roof, and first they recite the psalm "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psalms 19:2) in its entirety, in the melody used here in our city before the blessing of the [new] moon; then the psalm "Praise the Lord from the heavens" (ibid. 148); then these verses: "For the Lord God is a sun and shield; the Lord will give grace and glory; He will not withhold good from those who walk uprightly" (ibid. 84:12); "They shall fear You as long as the sun and before the moon, throughout all generations" (ibid. 72:5); "We give thanks to You, O God, we give thanks, for Your name is near; men tell of Your wondrous works" (ibid. 75:2); "But unto you who fear My name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings, and you shall go forth and grow up like calves of the stall" (Malachi 3:20); "Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, on the day that the Lord binds up the breach of His people and heals the wound of their injury" (Isaiah 30:26); and likewise he says, "and his lovers as the sun going forth in his might."

Afterward they say the portion of the fourth day [of creation], "And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heavens, etc." through "And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day" (Genesis 1:14-19), and afterward they say:

For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, etc. — behold, we come to give thanks to the Lord for the work of creation which He made, and to bless in His name the blessing which the Sages, of blessed memory, instituted for this day, over the sun at its turning point, which stands in the firmament at the beginning of its twenty-eight-year cycle, just as it began to stand on the fourth day of the six days of creation, in order to bring satisfaction to our Fashioner and to do the will of our Creator, to establish the root of this mitzvah of blessing in a high place; and may it rise before You as though we had directed in this mitzvah all the intentions fitting to be directed, and "may the pleasantness of the Lord our God, etc." [be upon us]. Afterward the entire congregation recites the blessing together, aloud, in joy and gladness, and the cantor recites the blessing after them by himself, alone, raising his voice, intending to discharge the obligation of the blind and the women who hear his voice.

Afterward they say the psalm (Psalms 136:26), "Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy endures forever," in its entirety, through "Give thanks to the God of heaven," in a pleasant melody; and afterward, "God, the Master over all works, blessed and praised, etc." through "and the holy Chayot"; afterward, "It is upon us to praise the Master of all, etc." through "the Lord shall be one and His name one"; and afterward the piyyut "Adon Olam asher malach, etc." [Lord of the world, who reigned...].

Afterward they say this petition: "May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers, that just as You have kept us alive and sustained us and brought us to this time to bless in it the blessing of the sun in Your name, so may You keep us alive and sustain us and grant us [to see] the turning of the sun in the years to come upon us, for a good life and for peace, rejoicing in the building of Your city and gladdened in Your service, and grant us to see the face of Your anointed one; and may there be fulfilled in our days the verse that is written (Isaiah 30:26), 'Moreover the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, on the day that the Lord binds up the breach of His people and heals the wound of their injury,' and 'may the pleasantness [of the Lord], etc.,' 'may they be acceptable, etc.'"; and afterward, "Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel, etc." (Mishnah, Makkot 23b); and afterward Kaddish 'al Yisrael.'

And I, the young author, will recount the kindnesses of the Lord, blessed be He, with which He favored me in this year, the year 5657 [1897], on the fifth day of the month of Nisan, which fell on the fourth day of the week, on the holy Sabbath, in a gathering of a great assembly, when we went up onto the roof of the Great Synagogue and, with the help of the Lord, blessed be He, performed [the order of the blessing] as we have written above; and many women also gathered there, and I myself recited the blessing in a loud voice, and intended to discharge the obligation of the women and the blind, as we explained above with the help of Heaven; and after the entire order mentioned, the congregation recited Kaddish 'al Yisrael,' and I stood and, with the help of the Lord, blessed be He, expounded on the matter of the mitzvah, for 'a word fitly spoken, how good it is.' May the Lord, blessed be He, in His mercy and kindness, grant us to recite the blessing of the sun in Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and established, which is destined to occur in the year 5685 [1925], in the month of Nisan, in which redemption and blessing and goodness shall increase for us and for all Israel and for the Holy Land; may our eyes see and our hearts rejoice at the coming of the redeemer, our righteous Messiah, speedily in our days, Amen, so may it be His will.

clarification.explanation:
One who sees the sun at its turning point [tekufah] — once every twenty-eight years, when the tekufah falls at the start of the night of Wednesday — recites upon seeing it in the morning, "Blessed... who performs the work of creation," since at that time the sun stands at the point where it stood at the beginning of its creation in the firmament. The time for the blessing with [God's] name and sovereignty is until three seasonal hours [into the day]; if that has passed — he recites it without name and sovereignty until midday (Chatam Sofer), and although some say to recite it with name and sovereignty until midday — in a case of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. He should be careful to recite the blessing in a place where he can see the disk of the sun itself, not merely see the light of its rising.
It is a mitzvah to recite it in a large gathering ("In the multitude of people is the King's glory"). If there was a cloud — he does not recite the blessing until it passes; if it does not pass — he recites it without [God's] name and sovereignty (even though many hold to recite it with name and sovereignty — in a case of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient). As for women, the Chatam Sofer raised the question whether they should recite it; therefore the women come and stand near the men, and the cantor recites the blessing aloud, intending to discharge their obligation (and likewise for the blind), and they intend to fulfill their obligation by hearing it. Shehecheyanu is not recited over this mitzvah (the Ketav Sofer gives a reason for this).
The order of the blessing is: the congregation and cantor stand together on the roof; first they recite the psalm "The heavens declare the glory of God," then "Praise the Lord from the heavens," then verses ("For the Lord God is a sun and shield," "They shall fear You as long as the sun," "We give thanks to You, O God," "the sun of righteousness shall arise," "the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun"); afterward the portion of the fourth day ("Let there be lights"); afterward "for the sake of the unification" and the formula of thanksgiving for the work of creation; then the entire congregation recites the blessing together, and the cantor repeats it alone aloud; afterward the psalm "Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good," "God, the Master over all works," "It is upon us to praise," the piyyut "Adon Olam," and afterward the petition "May it be Your will... so may You keep us alive... and grant us to see the face of Your anointed one," "Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya," and Kaddish "al Yisrael." The Ben Ish Chai relates that he merited to carry out this order in the year 5657, on the 5th of Nisan, which fell on the fourth day of the week, on the holy Sabbath, in a great gathering on the roof of the Great Synagogue, and he recited the blessing aloud and discharged the obligation of the women and the blind, and looks forward to reciting the blessing of the sun in Jerusalem in the year 5685.
takeaways: The blessing of the sun [Birkat HaChamah] is recited once every 28 years, on the morning of Wednesday: "who performs the work of creation," with [God's] name and sovereignty until three seasonal hours (afterward without name and sovereignty), facing the disk of the sun itself.
It is recited in a large gathering; in cloud cover — without name and sovereignty; women and the blind fulfill their obligation by hearing the cantor; there is no Shehecheyanu.
There is a complete order: psalms, verses, the portion of the fourth day, "for the sake of the unification," the blessing recited by the congregation and then the cantor, and petitions and Kaddish.
